questions.question: In a metric space $(\boldsymbol{X},d)$, what does it mean for $(\boldsymbol{x}_i)$ to converge to $\boldsymbol{x}$ under $d$?
questions.explanation: A sequence $(x_i)$ converges to $x$ under $d$ when $\lim_{i\to\infty} d(x_i,x)=0$: the distance from $x_i$ to $x$ tends to $0$ as $i\to\infty$.
questions.source_support: The definition states that $(\boldsymbol{x}_i)$ converges to $\boldsymbol{x}$ under $d$ if $\lim_{i\to\infty}d(\boldsymbol{x}_i,\boldsymbol{x}) = 0$.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: $d(x_i,x)=0$ for every $i$ would mean every $x_i=x$ (a constant sequence); convergence is weaker.
$d(x_i,x)$ being constant (e.g., always $1$) means no convergence to $x$; it must tend to $0$.
$x_i=x$ for infinitely many $i$ does not imply convergence; e.g., $a_n=(-1)^n$ equals $1$ for infinitely many $n$ but does not converge.
